lines: DM: As the ship begins to drift into the sky, heading south for the elven kingdom of Orenlas, an old dwarf sits in his cabin writing at a small desk in cramped dwarven runes:

DM: “4 Barukhelm 5881,” he writes. “My first adventure in more than a decade succeeded beyond my wildest imagination. That Seeker fellow sure knows how to pick his friends. I was not sure what to think when I first met them. They seemed rather prone to excessive chatter and terminal indecision. I was afraid it would be like being back on my travels with Lyrial and her friends. So much time sitting around debating, so little time doing. Although I guess it was in one of those rambling discourses that she told me about the Edge of Echoes in the first place. Once we got moving, I couldn't help but wonder at the powerful oddities they carried, and their skill at using them. A folding boat, I've seen, sure, but a mirror that reveals the history of things? That was a sight. And all Seeker's friends proved quite adept at battle. I think I would have been drowned by water elementals if they had not leapt to my defense.

DM: Oh, and flight. To fly again! It was nothing like the flying carpet we borrowed back in the day. To be able to think and just go where you wish—truly something else. Somehow the fey step trick I learned from Lyrial feels cheap in comparison now.
DM: Of course, my goal was to make my dear Pebblepeep fly, and I can't believe how successful I was. I surprise even myself sometimes. Aha!

DM: All that hard work outfitting this ship—oh, this ship! I wonder if they'd let me stay, or maybe even let me fly it someday—was well worth it. It'll be hard going back to life in Tollen after this.”

DM: I saw Pelois and Cekious, the twin emperors, die in dragon fire, but we prevailed and Drankor was saved, and it was worth saving in those days.
DM: During my first mela I returned to Rostaurë, where my son and my daughter were born. And they followed in my footsteps, traveling to Drankor and serving in the court of Imrodel.

DM: It was then that things started to go wrong. The Emperor Helea—she was assassinated by the Omnis Pura, and started starting a Civil war. My son was killed in the fighting in Drankor. My daughter fled with a small group hiding out in the hills to the west of the city, keeping a guerrilla resistance alive in Helea's name. But later she was killed as well.
DM: Protected as many as I could in the Rostaurë.
DM: Especially the peronar, the elves who had lived with humans since the days of Hkar, and were seen as particularly insidious and vile by the Omnis Pura.

DM: We were always protected by Aldanor's grace, by the power of his magic that ran through my arm and my blade.

DM: It was when Apollyon, then Emperor, betrayed a dragon, Cha'mutte—later, who we would fight against for our very survival—slaughtering the Orcs and stealing the cloak of rainbows from them, that things became dire.
DM: With the cloak, Aldanor's protection meant nothing. Apollyon sliced through the defenders of Rostaurë like a hot knife. Everywhere he strode, the power of Aldanor was quelled.
DM: The tricks that protected us ceased to matter. The city of Estemar was sacked. Rostaurë burned. The elder trees cut, sleeping children inside.

DM: And there was that day. I was watching. He stood and proclaimed himself a God. The firstborn of humans. And he raised the scepter. And there were people, as far as the eye could see, cheering and chanting his name.

DM: And I saw Apollyon choking on his hubris, staggering through this mist, looking for something.
DM: As I tried to flee the city and gather survivors, avoid what I could of the few of Apollyon's forces still clinging to life.

DM: I saw him laughing, standing on the steps of his palace, his arms withered—holds up her arm—as mine is now—raising this vial of pure blackness to his mouth. And cursing Cha'mutte. Do not know what happened after he drank, but I'm sure he did not die.

DM: And I swore then, as I turned with the survivors north, that I would not rest until Apollyon was dead.

DM: I tried to learn as much as I could about him and his fate. What had happened to him. Even when I felt the roots of Aldanor no longer pulling me to Taelgar, had something more immediate, more personal, to hold me to. That Apollyon must not be allowed to rise ever again. And then—
